title: The Onboarding Drop-Off
summary: Shopwell is an online store with its own mobile app — first-party retail, no marketplace or third-party sellers. Its customers are shoppers who install the app from ads and app-store features, and the company earns when they browse and buy.

Q1.text: Onboarding completion has dropped from 78% to 65% over the last month. What do you do?

choices.text: Review usability session recordings from the last month
choices.reveal: Most users who drop off pause noticeably on the permissions screen before leaving.

choices.text: Talk to users who recently abandoned onboarding
choices.reveal: Several users say they weren't sure why the app needed the permissions it asked for.
choices.because: The people who left can say why; their reasons are the fastest route to the cause.

choices.text: Check what changed in the onboarding flow recently
choices.reveal: A new permissions screen was added three weeks ago to support a location-based feature.

choices.text: Define what 'successful onboarding' should mean before investigating further
choices.reveal: Success was previously defined purely as 'reached the home screen,' with no measure of user understanding.

Q2.text: Users pause noticeably on the permissions screen before many of them leave. What do you investigate next?

choices.text: Break down drop-off by device type

reveal.text: On mobile, most drop-off happens on the permissions screen. On desktop, drop-off is spread evenly across all steps.

choices.because: The pause-then-leave pattern may not be uniform; splitting by device isolates where the failure actually lives.

choices.text: Review what the permissions screen currently communicates
choices.reveal: The screen lists the permissions requested but doesn't explain why they're needed or what happens if a user declines.

choices.text: Check whether declining a permission blocks onboarding entirely
choices.reveal: Declining any permission currently stops onboarding, with no way to continue.

Q3.text: Several users say they weren't sure why the app needed the permissions it asked for. What do you do next?

choices.text: Review what the permissions screen currently communicates
choices.reveal: The screen lists the permissions requested but doesn't explain why they're needed or what happens if a user declines.

choices.text: Check whether this is a new problem or a longstanding one
choices.reveal: The permissions screen was added three weeks ago; before that, onboarding didn't request these permissions at all.
choices.because: If the confusion started with the new screen, the cause is the screen — not the users.

choices.text: Define what information users need before granting a permission
choices.reveal: Users need to understand what the permission enables, what happens if they decline, and whether they can change their mind later.

Q4.text: A new permissions screen was added three weeks ago to support a location-based feature. What do you do next?

choices.text: Compare onboarding completion before and after the screen was added
choices.reveal: Completion was stable at 78% before the screen was added and has declined steadily since.
choices.because: Before/after data turns a coincidence into a cause.

choices.text: Check whether the permission is required or optional for core app use
choices.reveal: The location permission is only needed for one optional feature, not for the app's core functionality.

choices.text: Explore whether this permission request could happen later, in context
choices.reveal: Other permissions in the app are currently requested contextually, at the moment they're needed, except this one.

Q5.text: Success was previously defined only as 'reached the home screen,' with no measure of understanding. What do you do next?

choices.text: Investigate what users understand about the app right after onboarding
choices.reveal: In short follow-up surveys, many users who completed onboarding can't clearly explain what the location permission was for.

choices.text: Investigate where users hesitate during onboarding
choices.reveal: Most users who drop off pause noticeably on the permissions screen before leaving.
choices.because: Hesitation points at the exact step where the experience breaks down.

choices.text: Define what onboarding needs to achieve beyond completion
choices.reveal: Onboarding should leave users understanding what they agreed to and confident they can proceed.

Q6.text: Drop-off on the permissions screen is concentrated on mobile, while desktop drop-off is spread across all steps. What do you investigate next?

choices.text: Review how the permissions screen renders on mobile specifically
choices.reveal: On smaller screens, the explanation text is truncated, leaving only the permission name and two buttons visible.
choices.because: The mobile-specific failure deserves a mobile-specific look; that is where the concentration is.

choices.text: Investigate the general desktop drop-off separately
choices.reveal: Desktop drop-off appears linked to overall onboarding length, not any single screen.

choices.text: Check whether the permissions screen is mandatory on both platforms
choices.reveal: The permissions screen is mandatory on both platforms, with no option to skip and return later.

Q7.text: The permissions screen lists what's requested but doesn't explain why it's needed or what happens if declined. What do you do?

choices.text: Define the information users actually need at this step
choices.reveal: Users need to understand the purpose of the permission, the consequence of declining, and that the choice can be changed later.
choices.because: Naming what users must understand turns a vague complaint into a design requirement.

choices.text: Explore alternative ways to present this screen
choices.reveal: Options include an inline explanation, a contextual request tied to the relevant feature, or a benefit-led framing before the system prompt.

choices.text: Check how similar permission requests are handled elsewhere in the app
choices.reveal: Other permissions in the app are requested contextually, with a short explanation shown just before the system prompt.

Q8.text: Declining the permission currently blocks onboarding entirely, even though the permission is only needed for one optional feature. What do you do next?

choices.text: Define what should happen if a user declines
choices.reveal: If declined, users should be able to continue onboarding and enable the feature later from settings.
choices.because: Deciding the decline behavior is the product decision everything else serves.

choices.text: Explore letting users skip and continue onboarding
choices.reveal: Removing the hard block would require a way to re-prompt for the permission later, in context.

choices.text: Check with engineering whether the feature can degrade gracefully without the permission
choices.reveal: Engineering confirms the feature can be fully disabled without the permission, with no impact on the rest of the app.

Q9.text: You've defined what users need to understand before granting this permission. What do you do next?

choices.text: Explore how to communicate this at the right moment
choices.reveal: Two directions emerge: explain everything upfront in onboarding, or move the request to the moment the feature is first used.
choices.because: Where the request happens matters as much as what it says; explore timing first.

choices.text: Design a revised permissions screen with clearer explanation
choices.reveal: A revised screen adds a short explanation and a visible 'you can change this later' note.

choices.text: Investigate whether moving the request later is technically feasible
choices.reveal: Engineering confirms the permission can be requested contextually rather than during onboarding.

Q10.text: Two directions are on the table: keep the request in onboarding with better explanation, or move it to when the feature is first used. What do you do?

choices.text: Design both directions as low-fidelity concepts to compare
choices.reveal: The contextual version removes one full step from onboarding but requires a new prompt inside the feature itself.
choices.because: Comparing concepts side by side beats arguing in the abstract.

choices.text: Explore the trade-offs of each direction with stakeholders
choices.reveal: Engineering notes the contextual version is straightforward to build; analytics notes it will be harder to track permission grant rate against onboarding.

choices.text: Design the contextual version as the primary direction
choices.reveal: The contextual prompt appears the first time a user taps the location-based feature, with a short explanation and a system prompt.

Q11.text: Desktop drop-off appears tied to overall onboarding length rather than a single screen. What do you do next?

choices.text: Investigate which steps users spend the most time on
choices.reveal: Two steps account for most of the time spent: the permissions screen and a preferences-setup step.
choices.because: Two steps eat most of the time; measure before cutting.

choices.text: Explore reducing the number of required onboarding steps
choices.reveal: The preferences-setup step could be deferred to a later moment without blocking core app use.

choices.text: Define what must happen during onboarding versus what can happen later
choices.reveal: Only account creation and the location permission decision are strictly required upfront; everything else can be deferred.

Q12.text: You have a concrete design direction for the permissions request. What do you do before releasing it?

choices.text: Run a usability test comparing it to the current version
choices.reveal: Users understand the purpose of the permission significantly more often with the new version, and fewer hesitate before deciding.
choices.because: Only users can tell you whether the explanation actually lands.

choices.text: Review the direction with engineering and accessibility
choices.reveal: The design is technically feasible and passes an accessibility review, with one note about contrast on the explanation text.

choices.text: Test it with users who previously declined the permission
choices.reveal: Several previously-declining users say they would grant the permission now that they understand what it's for.

Q13.text: You're deciding between deferring parts of onboarding versus keeping the flow as-is with better explanations. What do you do?

choices.text: Prototype a shortened onboarding flow and test it
choices.reveal: A shortened flow tests well for completion, but a few users express uncertainty about whether onboarding is 'finished.'
choices.because: Test the shortened flow before committing to what gets cut.

choices.text: Design a version that clearly signals deferred steps can be completed later
choices.reveal: Adding a lightweight 'finish setup later' indicator addresses the completion-uncertainty concern from testing.

choices.text: Review the shortened flow with the design-system team
choices.reveal: The design-system team confirms the deferred-step pattern already exists elsewhere in the app and can be reused here.

Q14.text: The revised onboarding direction has been validated with users, engineering, and accessibility review. What do you do next?

choices.text: Release it gradually and monitor onboarding completion
choices.reveal: Onboarding completion recovers to 76% within two weeks of the gradual rollout.
choices.because: A gradual rollout with the metric you set out to fix closes the loop.

choices.text: Expand the rollout while monitoring post-onboarding understanding
choices.reveal: Follow-up surveys show a significant increase in users who can correctly explain what the permission is used for.

choices.text: Document the new pattern for reuse in future permission requests
choices.reveal: The pattern is added to the design system as the standard approach for contextual permission requests.

criteria.label: Finding the root cause
criteria.guidance: The drop has one trigger — name it before fixing anything.

criteria.label: Measuring before cutting
criteria.guidance: Before/after data turns a coincidence into a cause.

criteria.label: Designing for the human need
criteria.guidance: Understanding and the decline path are the product decision.

criteria.label: Proving the fix worked
criteria.guidance: Roll out against the metric you set out to fix.
